bio_ocra.1.2.summary: Enzymes are biological catalysts made of proteins that speed up metabolic reactions without being used up. Their unique active site binds specifically to complementary substrates via the lock-and-key mechanism, forming enzyme-substrate complexes. Enzyme activity is strictly regulated and affected by factors such as temperature and pH, which alter the shape of the active site through denaturation, or substrate concentration, which limits the rate of reaction.

core.h: Introduction to Enzymes as Biological Catalysts
core.p: Living organisms require thousands of chemical reactions to sustain life, collectively known as metabolism. Many of these reactions occur too slowly at normal body temperature to support life processes. Enzymes solve this problem by acting as biological catalysts.
bullets: Enzymes are proteins folded into complex 3D shapes.
They speed up chemical reactions by lowering the activation energy required.
They remain unchanged at the end of the reaction and can be reused repeatedly.
They are specific, meaning each enzyme catalyses only one particular reaction or type of reaction.

callouts.p: A biological catalyst, made of protein, that increases the rate of metabolic reactions without being consumed or permanently altered.
Enzymes work by lowering the activation energy, which is the minimum amount of energy particles need to collide and react.

fig.cap: Comparison of reaction energy profiles with and without an enzyme catalyst.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="50" y2="30" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="225" font-size="12" fill="#334155">Progress of reaction</text><text x="10" y="115" font-size="12" fill="#334155" transform="rotate(-90, 10, 115)">Energy</text><path d="M 50 180 Q 150 20 250 180" fill="none" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M 50 180 Q 150 110 250 180" fill="none" stroke="#22c55e" stroke-width="3"/><text x="260" y="90" font-size="11" fill="#22c55e">With enzyme</text><text x="260" y="50" font-size="11" fill="#ef4444">Without enzyme</text></svg>

core.h: The Active Site and Enzyme Specificity
core.p: Every enzyme molecule contains a very specific region called the active site. This is a cleft or depression on the surface of the enzyme where the reactant binds.
bullets: The shape of the active site is complementary to the shape of one specific substrate.
Only the correct substrate can fit into the active site, just like a specific key fits into a specific lock.
This lock-and-key model explains why amylase breaks down starch but cannot digest protein.
A slight change in the amino acid sequence alters the 3D shape, destroying the active site.

callouts.p: The unique region on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the chemical reaction takes place.
Always use the word 'complementary' when describing how the substrate fits the active site. Never say 'the substrate fits into the enzyme like a puzzle piece'.

fig.cap: The lock and key model showing enzyme specificity and the active site.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><rect x="80" y="60" width="120" height="120" rx="20" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1e40af" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 140 60 L 140 100 Q 140 110 130 110 L 110 110 Q 100 110 100 100 L 100 60" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#1e40af" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="45" font-size="12" fill="#1e40af">Enzyme (Active Site)</text><rect x="240" y="90" width="60" height="50" rx="10" fill="#fed7aa" stroke="#c2410c" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 270 90 L 270 100 Q 270 110 260 110 L 250 110 Q 240 110 240 100 L 240 90" fill="#fed7aa" stroke="#c2410c" stroke-width="2"/><text x="240" y="75" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">Substrate</text><line x1="210" y1="115" x2="230" y2="115" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/></svg>

core.p: When a substrate enters an enzyme's active site, they temporarily bind together to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
bullets: Substrate + Enzyme ⇌ Enzyme-Substrate Complex ⇌ Enzyme + Product(s).
The forces holding the substrate in place strain chemical bonds, making it easier for the reaction to occur.
Once the reaction is complete, the products no longer fit the active site and leave.
The enzyme is left unchanged and ready to bind with another substrate molecule.

callouts.p: The temporary structure formed when the substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme.

core.h: Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity
core.p: Temperature profoundly affects the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions due to changes in kinetic energy and protein structure.
bullets: As temperature increases from low values, kinetic energy increases, leading to more frequent successful collisions between enzyme and substrate.
The rate of reaction increases until it reaches the optimum temperature (typically around 37°C in humans).
Above the optimum temperature, excessive thermal energy causes atoms in the enzyme to vibrate violently.
This breaks the bonds holding the 3D tertiary structure together, permanently changing the shape of the active site.

callouts.p: The temperature at which an enzyme works at its maximum possible rate.
Never write that enzymes are 'killed'. Enzymes are molecules, not living cells. They are 'denatured'.

fig.cap: Graph showing the effect of temperature on enzyme activity, including optimum and denaturation.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="50" y2="30" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="230" font-size="12" fill="#334155">Temperature (°C)</text><text x="15" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#334155" transform="rotate(-90, 15, 120)">Rate of Reaction</text><path d="M 50 190 Q 180 20 330 195" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="180" y1="50" x2="180" y2="200" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="145" y="215" font-size="11" fill="#1e293b">Optimum</text></svg>

core.p: Denaturation is the irreversible structural alteration of a protein enzyme's active site, rendering it non-functional.
bullets: The active site loses its precise shape so the substrate can no longer bind.
Caused by temperatures significantly above the optimum or extreme pH levels.
No enzyme-substrate complexes can be formed once denaturation occurs.
The primary sequence of amino acids remains intact, but the secondary and tertiary folds are disrupted.

callouts.p: The permanent loss of the 3D tertiary structure of an enzyme, including the active site, due to extreme heat or pH.

core.h: Effect of pH on Enzyme Activity
core.p: pH is a measure of hydrogen ion concentration. Different enzymes have different optimum pH levels reflecting their natural environment.
bullets: Pepsin, found in the acidic stomach, has an optimum pH of around 2.
Amylase, found in the alkaline mouth and small intestine, has an optimum pH around 7 to 8.
Extreme changes in pH interfere with the ionic and hydrogen bonds holding the enzyme's 3D structure together.
This alters the shape of the active site, leading to denaturation and loss of enzyme activity.

callouts.p: Unlike temperature graphs which drop sharply to zero after the optimum, pH graphs are usually symmetrical bell curves.

core.h: Effect of Substrate Concentration on Enzyme Activity
core.p: Increasing substrate concentration affects the frequency of collisions between enzyme and substrate molecules.
bullets: At low substrate concentration, increasing substrate increases the rate of reaction because active sites are empty and available.
As substrate concentration continues to increase, all active sites eventually become saturated.
At this point, adding more substrate has no effect on the rate of reaction.
The maximum rate (Vmax) is reached, and the enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor.

callouts.p: When all enzyme active sites are occupied at any given moment, the rate of reaction reaches a plateau.

core.p: Required practical activity B4 involves investigating how factors such as pH, temperature, or substrate concentration affect enzyme activity.
bullets: A common experiment uses amylase to break down starch into maltose.
Iodine solution is used to test for the presence of starch at regular time intervals.
Starch turns blue-black with iodine; when it is fully digested to maltose, the iodine remains browny-orange.
The time taken for starch to disappear is recorded as a measure of the rate of reaction (Rate = 1 / time).

callouts.p: Use a water bath to maintain constant temperatures. Take readings every 30 seconds until iodine no longer changes colour.

core.p: To compare enzyme activity across different conditions, scientists calculate the rate of reaction from experimental data.
bullets: Rate can be calculated using the formula: Rate = Change / Time.
For volume of product formed over time: Rate = Volume (cm3) / Time (s).
For substrate disappearance time: Rate = 1 / Time (s-1) or 1000 / Time for easier numbers.
Ensure correct units are stated in exam answers, such as cm3 s-1.

callouts.p: Always double check your units when calculating rates. If time is in seconds, the rate unit is s-1.

core.h: Digestion and Enzymes in the Human Body
core.p: Enzymes play a vital role in digesting large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.
bullets: Carbohydrases (e.g., amylase) break down carbohydrates into simple sugars like glucose.
Proteases (e.g., pepsin, trypsin) break down proteins into amino acids.
Lipases break down lipids (fats and oils) into glycerol and fatty acids.
Digestive enzymes are produced by specialized cells in glands and the lining of the gut.

analogy.t: The Lock and Factory Worker Analogy
analogy.p: An enzyme is like a specialist factory machine designed to assemble or disassemble a specific component (the substrate). The machine has a precise slot (the active site) where only the matching raw material fits. Once processed, the finished item is ejected and the machine is ready for the next part. Where it breaks down: Unlike a real machine, enzymes do not have moving mechanical parts; their action relies entirely on random thermal collisions and molecular shape.

terms.d: The specific region on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the catalytic reaction occurs.
The minimum energy required by particles to initiate a chemical reaction.
A digestive enzyme that catalyses the breakdown of starch into maltose.
A substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed or altered.
The permanent loss of 3D tertiary structure of a protein enzyme, destroying the active site.
A biological catalyst made of protein that increases metabolic reaction rates.
The temporary intermediate formed when a substrate fits into an enzyme's active site.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
The sum total of all chemical reactions taking place within an organism.
The temperature at which an enzyme-catalysed reaction proceeds at its maximum rate.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids.
A measure of how fast reactants are used up or products are formed over time.
The restriction of an enzyme to catalysing only one specific reaction or substrate.
The reactant molecule upon which an enzyme acts.

mistakes.w: Enzymes are killed at high temperatures.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are molecules, not living organisms. They are denatured, not killed.

mistakes.w: The active site changes shape to fit the substrate perfectly.
mistakes.r: The active site is already complementary to the substrate shape.

mistakes.w: Enzymes get used up during a chemical reaction.
mistakes.r: Enzymes remain unchanged at the end of a reaction and can be reused.

mistakes.w: Denaturation is reversible if you cool the enzyme down.
mistakes.r: Denaturation involves the permanent breaking of bonds holding the 3D structure, so it is irreversible.

mistakes.w: Lowering temperature causes enzymes to denature.
mistakes.r: Low temperatures reduce kinetic energy and slow activity, but do not denature enzymes.

mistakes.w: Starch is broken down by protease.
mistakes.r: Starch is a carbohydrate, so it is broken down by amylase.

mistakes.w: Enzymes provide energy for chemical reactions.
mistakes.r: Enzymes do not supply energy; they lower the activation energy required.

exam.q: Define the term 'enzyme'.
model: A biological catalyst
Made of protein that speeds up metabolic reactions without being used up
exam.tip: Make sure you include both 'biological catalyst' and 'protein' to secure both marks.

exam.q: Explain why enzyme activity decreases at temperatures above the optimum.
model: Excessive heat causes atoms in the enzyme to vibrate too much
Bonds holding the 3D tertiary structure together break
The shape of the active site is permanently altered
The substrate is no longer complementary and can no longer bind (denaturation)
exam.tip: Use the word 'denatured' and explain the physical change to the active site for full marks.

exam.q: Describe the lock and key model of enzyme action.
model: The active site has a specific 3D shape
The substrate is complementary in shape to the active site
The substrate fits precisely into the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex
exam.tip: Always use the word 'complementary' when discussing the shape match.

exam.q: A student investigates the effect of pH on amylase. State two control variables they must maintain.
model: Temperature
Concentration of amylase (or volume of amylase / concentration of starch)
exam.tip: Name specific variables related to the practical rather than generic answers.

exam.q: Explain the effect of increasing substrate concentration on the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction.
model: As substrate concentration increases, rate increases because more enzyme-substrate complexes form
Eventually all active sites become saturated
Further increases in substrate concentration have no effect on the rate
exam.tip: Mention the plateau and active site saturation for the final mark.

exam.q: Name the products formed when lipids are broken down by lipase.
model: Glycerol
Fatty acids
exam.tip: Both products must be named correctly.

exam.q: Explain why pepsin works best at pH 2.
model: pH 2 is the optimum pH for pepsin
It matches the acidic environment of the stomach where pepsin is naturally found
exam.tip: Link the pH value to the biological location in the body.

exam.q: Describe how iodine solution is used in the PAG B4 practical to find the time taken for starch breakdown.
model: Samples are taken from the reaction mixture at regular time intervals
Added to iodine solution in a spotting tile
Record the time when iodine remains orange/brown instead of turning blue-black
exam.tip: State both the initial colour and the final colour for clarity.

exam.q: Explain why lowering the temperature from 37°C to 5°C reduces enzyme activity without denaturing the enzyme.
model: Particles have lower kinetic energy at low temperatures
Fewer successful collisions occur between enzyme and substrate per unit time
exam.tip: Distinguish clearly between low temperature slowing activity and high temperature causing denaturation.

worked.q: In an experiment investigating amylase activity, 2 cm3 of starch solution was broken down completely in 40 seconds. Calculate the rate of reaction.
steps: Identify the formula for rate of reaction using volume and time: Rate = Volume / Time.
Substitute the given values into the formula: Rate = 2 / 40.
Calculate the final value: 0.05.
Add appropriate units: cm3 s-1.

worked.q: A student measures the time taken for amylase to break down starch at different temperatures. At 30°C, the reaction takes 50 seconds. Calculate the rate of reaction using Rate = 1 / time.
steps: Identify the formula: Rate = 1 / Time.
Substitute the time value: Rate = 1 / 50.
Calculate the decimal value: 0.02.
State the unit: s-1.

bio_ocra.1.0.summary: These comprehensive revision notes cover DNA structure, polymers, nucleotides, complementary base pairing, and the DNA extraction practical required for OCR GCSE Biology B1.2. They provide Grade 9 depth by explaining the chemical bonding, spatial arrangement of the double helix, and exact step-by-step methodology for isolating DNA from plant tissue. Every detail is aligned strictly with the OCR mark schemes to ensure maximum marks in the exam.

core.p: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is a large and complex molecule that carries genetic information inside the nucleus of cells. It is classified as a polymer, meaning it is built by joining together many smaller identical units called monomers. In DNA, these repeating monomer units are called nucleotides.
bullets: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid and is found in the nucleus.
It is a polymer built from repeating monomer units called nucleotides.
A polymer is a large molecule made from many smaller sub-units bonded together.
The backbone of the polymer provides structural strength and protects the genetic code.

callouts.p: A large molecule made from many smaller repeating units (monomers) joined together by covalent bonds.

core.p: Every individual nucleotide in a DNA molecule is constructed from three distinct chemical components bonded together. Understanding these three parts is essential for explaining how the overall polymer is assembled.
bullets: A phosphate group containing phosphorus and oxygen atoms.
A pentose (5-carbon) sugar called deoxyribose.
A nitrogenous base attached to the 1' carbon of the sugar.
The sugar and phosphate groups alternate to form the strong structural backbone of the DNA strand.

callouts.p: Phosphate group + Deoxyribose sugar + Nitrogenous base.

fig.cap: Diagram of a single DNA nucleotide showing the three core components: phosphate, deoxyribose sugar, and a nitrogenous base.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><rect x="50" y="80" width="80" height="80" rx="10" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="90" y="125" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Phosphate</text><rect x="160" y="80" width="80" height="80" rx="10" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="115" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Deoxyribose</text><text x="200" y="135" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Sugar</text><rect x="270" y="80" width="80" height="80" rx="10" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="310" y="115" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Nitrogenous</text><text x="310" y="135" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Base</text><line x1="130" y1="120" x2="160" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="240" y1="120" x2="270" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

core.p: The genetic code is determined by the sequence of four different nitrogenous bases attached to the sugar-phosphate backbone. These bases belong to two structural categories: purines and pyrimidines, though knowing their exact chemical class is extra detail beyond basic GCSE.
bullets: Adenine, abbreviated as the letter A.
Thymine, abbreviated as the letter T.
Cytosine, abbreviated as the letter C.
Guanine, abbreviated as the letter G.

callouts.p: Remember AT and CG: **A**pples on **T**rees, **C**ars in **G**arages.

core.p: The bases across the two strands of DNA do not pair up randomly. Instead, specific bases form hydrogen bonds with each other based on their chemical structure and size. This is known as complementary base pairing.
bullets: Adenine (A) always pairs exclusively with Thymine (T).
Cytosine (C) always pairs exclusively with Guanine (G).
A and T form two hydrogen bonds between them.
C and G form three hydrogen bonds between them, making the C-G pairing slightly more stable.

callouts.p: The specific way in which the nitrogenous bases pair up: A with T, and C with G.

fig.cap: Complementary base pairing showing two strands held together by hydrogen bonds between A-T and C-G.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><rect x="80" y="40" width="40" height="30" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="60" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">A</text><rect x="280" y="40" width="40" height="30" fill="#fed7aa" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="300" y="60" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">T</text><line x1="120" y1="55" x2="280" y2="55" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="80" y="100" width="40" height="30" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="120" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">C</text><rect x="280" y="100" width="40" height="30" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="300" y="120" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">G</text><line x1="120" y1="115" x2="280" y2="115" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 60 20 L 60 220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M 340 20 L 340 220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="4"/><text x="200" y="200" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Dashed lines represent hydrogen bonds</text></svg>

core.p: DNA is not a flat, straight ladder; it is twisted into a 3D shape known as a double helix. This structure was discovered by James Watson, Francis Crick, Rosalind Franklin, and Maurice Wilkins.
bullets: Two polynucleotide strands coil around each other.
The shape resembles a twisted ladder or a spiral staircase.
The sugar-phosphate backbones form the outside structural rails.
The paired nitrogenous bases form the rungs on the inside of the helix.

callouts.p: Two strands of DNA wound together into a spiral shape, protected by the outer sugar-phosphate backbone.

fig.cap: The DNA double helix showing twisted backbones and internal base rungs.

core.p: DNA extraction is a standard practical technique used to isolate DNA from plant cells so it can be seen and studied. Plant tissue like kiwi fruit or strawberries is commonly used because they yield large amounts of DNA.
bullets: Cell walls must be broken down physically and chemically to release cell contents.
Cell membranes and nuclear membranes must be dissolved using detergent.
Proteins associated with DNA must be broken down using enzymes.
Precipitation using ice-cold alcohol allows the DNA to become visible as a white precipitate.

callouts.p: Never use hot alcohol or heat the mixture after adding ethanol, as this will denature and destroy the extracted DNA.

core.h: 7. Step 1: Crushing and Breaking Cell Walls
core.p: The first practical step in extracting DNA is to disrupt the tough plant cell walls mechanically. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, which protects the inner cell components.
bullets: Take a peeled kiwi fruit or strawberry and mash it using a pestle and mortar.
This mechanical crushing breaks open the rigid cellulose cell walls.
Increasing the surface area makes it easier for chemical solutions to penetrate.
Do not grind too violently or you will shear and break the long DNA molecules into tiny fragments.

callouts.p: Crushing fruit breaks cell walls to release cell contents into solution.

core.p: Once cells are crushed, cell membranes and nuclear membranes still enclose the DNA. Cell membranes are made of lipids (fats), which require a detergent to break them down.
bullets: Add a solution containing washing-up liquid (detergent) and salt to the mashed fruit.
The detergent molecules disrupt and emulsify the lipid bilayers of cell and nuclear membranes.
This releases the DNA out into the liquid filtrate.
The salt (sodium chloride) neutralises negative charges on the DNA strands, causing them to clump together easily.

callouts.p: Emulsifies and breaks down lipid cell membranes to release DNA into the solution.

core.p: After mixing with detergent and salt, the mixture contains cellular debris, large pieces of fruit tissue, and the liquid filtrate containing dissolved DNA.
bullets: Pour the mixture through a piece of muslin cloth or filter paper placed in a funnel.
Collect the clear or translucent liquid filtrate in a clean test tube.
This step removes unwanted solid plant debris and insoluble cellular parts.
The filtrate now contains the soluble DNA along with dissolved proteins and carbohydrates.

callouts.p: Do not squeeze the muslin cloth too hard, or cloudy pulp will pass through and contaminate your filtrate.

core.p: DNA in the nucleus is tightly wrapped around proteins called histones. To obtain pure DNA, these proteins must be removed from the solution.
bullets: Add a few drops of protease enzyme (like meat tenderiser or trypsin) to the filtrate.
Protease catalyses the breakdown of proteins into amino acids.
This separates the proteins from the DNA strands.
Proteins would otherwise interfere with viewing or testing the isolated DNA.

callouts.p: Digests and removes proteins attached to the DNA.

core.h: 11. Step 5: Precipitating DNA with Ice-Cold Ethanol
core.p: DNA is soluble in water, but it is completely insoluble in cold ethanol (alcohol). This chemical property allows scientists to pull the dissolved DNA out of solution.
bullets: Tilt the test tube and gently pour ice-cold ethanol down the inside wall of the tube.
Ethanol forms a distinct layer sitting on top of the aqueous fruit filtrate.
DNA precipitates (comes out of solution) right at the boundary between the water and alcohol layers.
The precipitated DNA appears as a stringy, white, fibrous mass that can be spooled onto a glass rod.

callouts.p: Ethanol must be ice-cold to maximise DNA precipitation and prevent any remaining enzyme activity.

fig.cap: DNA extraction test tube showing layers of fruit filtrate and ice-cold ethanol with precipitated white DNA at the interface.

analogy.t: The Spiral Staircase and Blueprint Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine DNA as a spiral staircase in a grand library. The handrails of the staircase represent the alternating sugar-phosphate backbone holding everything together. The steps you walk on represent the pairs of nitrogenous bases, where specific steps only fit together (A with T, C with G). The entire staircase acts as a master blueprint book containing coded instructions to build every protein in your body. This analogy breaks down because DNA is a dynamic, microscopic chemical polymer that unzips and replicates, unlike a static wooden staircase.

terms.d: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the polymer that stores genetic information in living organisms.

mistakes.w: Saying DNA is a protein or a cell.
mistakes.r: DNA is a nucleic acid polymer, not a protein or a whole cell.

mistakes.w: Stating Adenine pairs with Cytosine.
mistakes.r: Adenine always pairs with Thymine (A-T and C-G).

mistakes.w: Confusing sugar and phosphate positions in nucleotides.
mistakes.r: The base attaches to the sugar, and sugars and phosphates form the alternating backbone.

mistakes.w: Claiming ethanol dissolves DNA.
mistakes.r: Ethanol causes DNA to precipitate (insoluble), which is why it separates out.

mistakes.w: Heating the ethanol during DNA extraction.
mistakes.r: Ethanol must be ice-cold; heat denatures DNA and ruins the extraction.

mistakes.w: Calling the monomer a base instead of a nucleotide.
mistakes.r: The monomer is a nucleotide; the base is only one component of it.

mistakes.w: Writing that bonds between bases are strong covalent bonds.
mistakes.r: Bases are held together by weak hydrogen bonds.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the role of detergent in PAG B2.
mistakes.r: Detergent breaks down lipid cell membranes and nuclear membranes.

exam.q: State the three components that make up a single DNA nucleotide.
model: Phosphate group (1)
Deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base (1)
exam.tip: Mention all three distinct chemical parts for full marks.

exam.q: Describe the pairing rules for nitrogenous bases in a DNA molecule.
model: Adenine pairs with Thymine (1)
Cytosine pairs with Guanine (1)
exam.tip: Ensure you pair the correct letters together.

exam.q: Explain why ice-cold ethanol is added during the extraction of DNA from plant tissue (PAG B2).
model: DNA is insoluble in cold ethanol (1)
This causes the DNA to precipitate/separate out of solution so it becomes visible (1)
exam.tip: Always link ethanol to DNA insolubility.

exam.q: Describe the 3D structure of a DNA molecule.
model: Double helix (1)
Two strands twisted around each other / spiral shape (1)
exam.tip: Use the exact term 'double helix'.

exam.q: What is the function of detergent added to plant tissue during DNA extraction?
model: Breaks down/dissolves cell membranes (1)
And breaks down nuclear membranes to release DNA (1)
exam.tip: Detergent targets lipids in membranes.

exam.q: Name the type of bonds that hold complementary base pairs together in DNA.
model: Hydrogen bonds (1)
exam.tip: Do not write covalent or ionic bonds.

exam.q: A sample of DNA contains 22% Adenine. Calculate the percentage of Guanine in the same sample.
model: Adenine equals Thymine, so Thymine is also 22%, total 44% (1)
Remaining 56% split equally between C and G, so Guanine is 28% (1)
exam.tip: Remember A=T and C=G, and total equals 100%.

exam.q: Explain why protease enzyme is sometimes added during the DNA extraction practical.
model: Protease breaks down proteins (1)
That are bound to the DNA / histone proteins, purifying the DNA sample (1)
exam.tip: Link protease to protein digestion.

exam.q: Describe how plant cell walls are disrupted at the start of DNA extraction.
model: By crushing/mashing the plant tissue using a pestle and mortar (1)
This mechanical action breaks open the rigid cellulose cell walls (1)
exam.tip: Mention mechanical crushing or pestle and mortar.

exam.q: Explain why the sugar-phosphate backbone is important for the DNA molecule.
model: It provides structural strength/support to the strand (1)
It protects the reactive nitrogenous base sequence on the inside (1)
exam.tip: Think about structural protection of genetic code.

worked.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA was analysed and found to have 30% Cytosine bases. Calculate the percentage of Adenine bases in the sample.
steps: Step 1: Use complementary base pairing rules. Cytosine (C) always pairs with Guanine (G), so if Cytosine is 30%, Guanine must also be 30%.
Step 2: Add Cytosine and Guanine percentages together: 30% + 30% = 60%.
Step 3: Subtract this total from 100% to find the remaining percentage for Adenine and Thymine: 100% - 60% = 40%.
Step 4: Since Adenine (A) always equals Thymine (T) in amount, divide 40% by 2 to find Adenine: 40% / 2 = 20%.

worked.q: In an experiment extracting DNA from 10g of kiwi fruit, a student obtained 0.5g of purified DNA precipitate. Calculate the percentage yield of DNA by mass.
steps: Step 1: Identify the formula for percentage yield: (Mass of extracted DNA / Initial mass of tissue) x 100.
Step 2: Substitute the known values into the equation: (0.5g / 10g) x 100.
Step 3: Calculate the decimal value: 0.5 / 10 = 0.05.
Step 4: Multiply by 100 to convert to a percentage: 0.05 x 100 = 5%.

bio_ocra.1.1.summary: Protein synthesis is the two-stage process by which the genetic information stored in DNA is used to build functional proteins. It involves transcription, where a messenger RNA (mRNA) copy of a gene is made in the nucleus, and translation, where ribosomes in the cytoplasm read the mRNA sequence in triplets to assemble amino acids in a specific order. This precise sequence of amino acids determines how the protein folds into a unique 3D shape, which is essential for its specific biological function as an enzyme, hormone, or structural component.

core.p: DNA carries the instructions for life in the sequence of its bases (A, T, C, and G). A group of **three bases** is known as a **triplet**. Each triplet codes for one specific **amino acid**. Because there are four different bases, there are 64 possible triplet combinations (4x4x4), which is more than enough to code for the 20 different amino acids used by living organisms.
bullets: The code is non-overlapping: each base is only part of one triplet.
The sequence of triplets determines the sequence of amino acids.
The sequence of amino acids determines the final shape and function of the protein.

callouts.p: A sequence of three bases in DNA that codes for a specific amino acid during protein synthesis.

core.p: DNA is a very large molecule found in the **nucleus** of eukaryotic cells. It is too big to leave the nucleus through the nuclear pores. However, proteins are synthesised at the **ribosomes**, which are located in the cytoplasm. To solve this, the cell makes a smaller, mobile copy of the gene called **mRNA**.
bullets: DNA stays protected in the nucleus.
mRNA acts as a messenger between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
mRNA is single-stranded and shorter than DNA.

fig.cap: The flow of genetic information from the protected DNA in the nucleus to the protein-making machinery in the cytoplasm.

core.p: Transcription is the first stage of protein synthesis. It occurs in the nucleus. An enzyme called **RNA polymerase** binds to a region of non-coding DNA in front of a gene. It then moves along the DNA, unzipping the strands and building a complementary strand of mRNA.
bullets: The DNA strands unzip to expose the bases.
RNA polymerase uses one DNA strand as a template.
Free RNA nucleotides pair with the DNA bases.
In RNA, the base **Uracil (U)** replaces Thymine (T) and pairs with Adenine (A).

callouts.p: DNA A pairs with RNA U; DNA T pairs with RNA A; DNA C pairs with RNA G; DNA G pairs with RNA C.

core.p: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is a polymer of nucleotides, similar to DNA, but with three key differences that allow it to function as a temporary messenger.

Once the mRNA molecule is complete, it leaves the nucleus and enters the cytoplasm, where it attaches to a **ribosome**. This is where translation occurs: the 'language' of nucleic acids is translated into the 'language' of proteins (amino acids).
bullets: The ribosome moves along the mRNA strand.
It 'reads' the mRNA in groups of three bases called **codons**.
Each codon codes for one specific amino acid.

fig.cap: Transcription: RNA polymerase unzipping DNA and creating a complementary mRNA strand using base-pairing rules.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M20 40 Q100 40 150 100 Q200 160 380 160" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 160 Q100 160 150 100 Q200 40 380 40" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="100" rx="60" ry="40" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="115" y="105" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540">RNA Polymerase</text><path d="M160 105 L300 105" stroke="#fecaca" stroke-width="4"/><text x="200" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Growing mRNA strand</text><text x="30" y="30" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">DNA Strand</text></svg>

core.p: **Transfer RNA (tRNA)** molecules are the 'translators'. Each tRNA molecule carries a specific **amino acid** to the ribosome. At the other end of the tRNA is an **anticodon**—a sequence of three bases that is complementary to a codon on the mRNA.
bullets: tRNA molecules ensure the correct amino acid is brought for each codon.
The anticodon on the tRNA binds to the codon on the mRNA by complementary base pairing.
This ensures the amino acids are lined up in the exact order dictated by the DNA.

core.p: As the ribosome moves along the mRNA, it brings together the mRNA and the correct tRNA molecules. The amino acids carried by the tRNA molecules are joined together by **peptide bonds** to form a long chain called a **polypeptide**.
bullets: The first tRNA binds to the first codon.
The second tRNA binds to the next codon.
A bond forms between the two amino acids.
The first tRNA leaves to collect another amino acid, and the ribosome moves forward.

fig.cap: Translation: The ribosome reading mRNA codons and tRNA molecules delivering the correct amino acids to build a polypeptide chain.

core.p: A polypeptide chain is not yet a functional protein. Once the chain is complete, it detaches from the ribosome and **folds** into a specific three-dimensional shape. This shape is determined entirely by the sequence of amino acids.
bullets: Chemical interactions (like hydrogen bonds) between amino acids cause the chain to fold.
The 3D shape creates specific features like the **active site** of an enzyme.
If the sequence of amino acids is wrong, the protein may fold incorrectly and fail to function.

core.p: The final shape of the protein allows it to carry out its specific job in the cell. The variety of shapes possible allows proteins to perform many different roles.

Example/Function
Importance of Shape
rows: Active site must match the substrate.
Must fit into specific receptors on target cells.

core.p: The entire process can be summarised as: **DNA -> Transcription -> mRNA -> Translation -> Polypeptide -> Folding -> Protein**. Every step is controlled and precise to ensure the cell produces the exact proteins it needs at the right time.

callouts.p: Students often swap the names 'transcription' and 'translation'. Remember: Transcription comes first (C before L) and involves 'scripting' (writing) the mRNA copy.

analogy.p: Imagine the DNA is a huge, fragile Master Recipe Book kept in a library (the nucleus) that cannot be taken out. To make a cake (the protein), you must first make a photocopy of the specific recipe (mRNA). You take this photocopy to the kitchen (the ribosome). In the kitchen, the chef (ribosome) reads the instructions. Assistants (tRNA) bring the specific ingredients (amino acids) in the exact order listed. The ingredients are mixed to form a batter (polypeptide), which is then baked into a specific shape (folding) to become a cake. The analogy breaks down because, in a cell, the 'ingredients' are linked together in a chain, whereas in a cake, they are blended into a uniform mixture.

terms.d: The process of making an mRNA copy of a DNA gene sequence.
The process where ribosomes use the mRNA code to assemble amino acids into a polypeptide.
Messenger RNA; a single-stranded molecule that carries the genetic code from the nucleus to the ribosome.
Transfer RNA; molecules that transport specific amino acids to the ribosome during translation.
A sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for a single amino acid.
A sequence of three bases on a tRNA molecule that is complementary to an mRNA codon.
The enzyme responsible for unzipping DNA and joining RNA nucleotides during transcription.
The building blocks of proteins.
A long chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
The organelle in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis (translation) takes place.
The nitrogenous base found in RNA that replaces Thymine.
Regions of DNA that do not code for proteins but can control gene expression by providing binding sites for RNA polymerase.

mistakes.w: DNA leaves the nucleus to go to the ribosome.
mistakes.r: DNA is too large to leave the nucleus; an mRNA copy is made instead.

mistakes.w: Transcription happens in the cytoplasm.
mistakes.r: Transcription happens in the nucleus; translation happens in the cytoplasm/ribosome.

mistakes.w: The bases in DNA are the amino acids.
mistakes.r: Bases are part of nucleotides; three bases (a triplet) code for one amino acid.

mistakes.w: mRNA has Thymine (T).
mistakes.r: mRNA contains Uracil (U) instead of Thymine.

mistakes.w: Proteins are made of glucose.
mistakes.r: Proteins are made of amino acids; starch/cellulose are made of glucose.

mistakes.w: The ribosome makes the mRNA.
mistakes.r: RNA polymerase makes mRNA; the ribosome uses mRNA to make proteins.

mistakes.w: A single base codes for an amino acid.
mistakes.r: It takes a triplet (three bases) to code for one amino acid.

exam.q: Explain why the sequence of bases in a gene is important for the function of an enzyme.
model: The sequence of bases determines the sequence of amino acids.
The sequence of amino acids determines how the protein folds.
This creates a specific 3D shape.
Which forms a specific active site that is complementary to a substrate.
exam.tip: Always link 'base sequence' to 'amino acid sequence' and then to 'protein shape'.

exam.q: Describe the role of RNA polymerase in protein synthesis.
model: It binds to non-coding DNA in front of a gene.
It joins RNA nucleotides together to form an mRNA strand.
exam.tip: Mention its binding site and its role in building the polymer.

exam.q: State the names of the two main stages of protein synthesis.
model: Transcription
Translation
exam.tip: Spell these correctly; they are very similar.

exam.q: A DNA triplet is GCA. State the complementary mRNA codon.
model: CGU
exam.tip: Remember A pairs with U in RNA, not T.

exam.q: Describe what happens during translation.
model: mRNA attaches to a ribosome.
tRNA molecules bring specific amino acids.
The tRNA anticodon binds to the complementary mRNA codon.
Amino acids are joined together to form a polypeptide chain.
exam.tip: Focus on the ribosome, tRNA, and the growing chain.

exam.q: Explain why mRNA is needed for protein synthesis.
model: DNA is too large to leave the nucleus.
mRNA is small enough to travel to the ribosome in the cytoplasm.
exam.tip: Think about the physical locations of DNA and ribosomes.

exam.q: How many bases code for 5 amino acids?
exam.tip: Multiply the number of amino acids by 3.

exam.q: What determines the order in which amino acids are joined together?
model: The sequence of bases (or codons) in the mRNA.
exam.tip: The mRNA sequence is the direct template for translation.

exam.q: Describe the role of tRNA in translation.
model: It carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome.
Its anticodon matches the codon on the mRNA to ensure the correct order.
exam.tip: tRNA is the 'bridge' between the code and the amino acid.

worked.q: A section of mRNA has the sequence: AUG CGU GGC. Using a genetic code table, a student finds these code for Methionine, Arginine, and Glycine. If the DNA sequence changed from GGC to GGT, explain the likely effect on the protein.
steps: Identify the original DNA triplet: GGC.
Identify the new DNA triplet: GGT.
Determine the new mRNA codon: CCA (complementary to GGT).
State that a different codon may code for a different amino acid.
Conclude that if the amino acid changes, the protein shape/function might change.
worked.ans: The mutation changes the DNA triplet, which changes the mRNA codon to CCA. This may result in a different amino acid being added to the chain. This change in the amino acid sequence could cause the protein to fold differently, potentially altering its function or active site.

worked.q: Compare the structures of DNA and mRNA.
steps: Compare the number of strands.
Compare the type of sugar present.
Compare the nitrogenous bases used.
worked.ans: DNA is double-stranded forming a double helix, whereas mRNA is single-stranded. DNA contains the sugar deoxyribose, while mRNA contains ribose. Finally, DNA uses the base Thymine (T), which is replaced by Uracil (U) in mRNA.
